computer-systems.title: Memory and Storage
computer-systems.description: RAM, ROM, cache, registers, volatile vs non-volatile, secondary storage types and cloud storage.
computer-systems.content_html:
Primary and Secondary Storage

Computers use two broad categories of storage. Primary storage (also called main memory) is directly accessible by the CPU and is used for data and instructions the computer is currently working with. Secondary storage is separate from main memory and holds data long-term, even when the power is off. The CPU cannot access secondary storage directly — data must first be loaded into primary storage before the CPU can process it.

Key Fact

The four types of primary storage are: RAM (main working memory, volatile), ROM (startup instructions, non-volatile), cache (fast small memory on or near the CPU) and registers (the fastest storage, inside the CPU itself). RAM and ROM are the two you will be asked to compare most often.

Volatile and Non-Volatile Memory

A critical distinction in storage is whether memory retains its contents without power. Volatile memory is erased when power is cut. Non-volatile memory keeps its contents without power. RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile. This is why unsaved work is lost in a power cut — it exists only in volatile RAM.

RAM — Random Access Memory

RAM is the computer’s main working memory. When you open an application, the operating system copies it from secondary storage into RAM so the CPU can access it quickly. RAM is much faster than any form of secondary storage but loses everything when the computer is switched off.

The amount of RAM affects how many programs can be open at once without slowing down. A computer with more RAM can hold more data in quick-access memory, reducing the need to fetch from slower secondary storage. Modern computers typically have between 8 and 64 GB of RAM.

ROM — Read Only Memory

ROM stores the firmware instructions that run when the computer first powers on. These instructions initialise the hardware and begin loading the operating system from secondary storage into RAM. ROM is non-volatile and read-only in normal use, so its contents cannot be accidentally overwritten.

ROM is much smaller than RAM — it needs to hold only the minimal startup code, not entire programs. A computer’s ROM might contain just a few megabytes, whereas RAM is measured in gigabytes.

RAM: Volatile (loses contents without power)  |  Read and write  |  Stores currently running programs and data  |  Typically 8–64 GB in modern systems  |  Contents change constantly during use.

ROM: Non-volatile (retains contents without power)  |  Read-only in normal use  |  Stores startup firmware/boot instructions  |  Very small (typically a few MB)  |  Contents are fixed at manufacture.

Why Is Secondary Storage Needed?

Secondary storage is essential because RAM is volatile — switch the computer off and all RAM contents are gone. Secondary storage provides three things that primary storage cannot: persistence (files survive when power is off), capacity (far more data can be stored, measured in terabytes) and portability (storage devices can be moved between computers).

Every file you save, every application installed, and the operating system itself live on secondary storage. When you open a file, it is copied from secondary storage into RAM. When you save, it is written back from RAM to secondary storage.

Key Fact

Secondary storage is needed for three reasons: capacity (far more data than RAM can hold), persistence (data is retained without power) and portability (storage devices can be transported and used in other systems). RAM is fast but temporary; secondary storage is slower but permanent.

Types of Secondary Storage

Magnetic storage uses magnetic fields to encode data on a surface. Hard disk drives (HDDs) store data on rapidly spinning metal platters coated with a magnetic material. A read/write head moves across the spinning surface to access or record data. Magnetic tape is an older form used for archival backup — sequential access makes it slow to retrieve specific files but it can store very large amounts at low cost.

Solid-state storage (SSD) stores data in electronic memory chips with no moving parts. Because nothing physically moves, SSDs are faster, quieter, lighter and more shock-resistant than HDDs. However, SSDs cost more per gigabyte of capacity. Smartphones, tablets and modern laptops commonly use SSDs.

SSD advantages: Faster access times (no moving parts to position), silent, uses less power, more durable (resistant to physical shock), lighter and more compact.

SSD disadvantages: More expensive per GB, capacity per pound spent is lower than HDD, limited write cycles (though this is not a practical issue for typical usage).

HDD advantages: Lower cost per GB, available in very large capacities (multiple TB), widely available.

HDD disadvantages: Slower access (mechanical parts must physically move to the right position), produces heat and noise, vulnerable to physical shock (head crash), heavier and larger.

Cloud Storage

Cloud storage means storing files on servers owned and managed by a third party, accessed over the internet. Services such as these are used by millions of people and businesses to back up files, share data across devices and collaborate remotely.

Advantages of cloud storage: Files are accessible from any device with internet access, data is backed up automatically (protection against local hardware failure), easy to share files with others, and no physical hardware to manage or replace.

Disadvantages of cloud storage: Requires an internet connection to access files, dependent on the service provider remaining operational, raises privacy concerns (data is held by a third party), and ongoing subscription costs can be higher long-term than purchasing local storage. Access can be slower than local storage if internet speeds are limited.

computer-systems.title: Software, Programming Languages and Translators
computer-systems.description: System vs application software, low- vs high-level languages, and compilers, interpreters and assemblers.
computer-systems.content_html:
Hardware and Software

Hardware is the physical equipment that makes up a computer. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. Neither is useful without the other: the most powerful processor in the world does nothing without software to direct it, and the cleverest program needs hardware to run on.

Key Fact

All software falls into one of two categories: system software, which manages the computer’s resources and provides a platform for other software to run, and application software, which performs tasks directly for the end user.

System Software

System software sits between the hardware and the user. It handles the low-level work that applications rely on. The three main types are the operating system, utility programs, and device drivers.

An operating system (OS) manages five key areas: the processor (deciding which programs get CPU time), memory (allocating RAM to programs as they open), input/output devices (communicating with keyboards, screens, printers), applications (providing services applications need, such as file access), and security (managing user accounts and access permissions). Without the OS, every application would need to include its own code for all of these — an impossible duplication of effort.

Utility programs carry out maintenance tasks. A file compression tool reduces the size of files before they are transferred; a disk cleanup tool removes temporary files to free up space; encryption software scrambles data so it cannot be read if intercepted. These are distinct from applications because they serve the system itself rather than the user’s primary tasks.

Application Software

Application software is what most people think of when they think of a program: a web browser, a word processor, a banking app, a game. Applications depend entirely on system software — they request services from the OS rather than communicating with hardware directly. This separation keeps development manageable: a game developer writes code to draw a window and play sound, and the OS handles the rest.

A common exam error is to describe an antivirus program as application software. It is a utility (system software) because its purpose is to maintain the health of the system, not to help the user complete a personal task. Similarly, a device driver is system software — the user never directly interacts with it, but the OS uses it to communicate with a printer or graphics card. Application software, by contrast, is always directly task-facing: photo editing, messaging, spreadsheets.

Programming Languages: Low-Level and High-Level

Processors can only execute instructions written in machine code — patterns of 0s and 1s. Writing in machine code directly is extremely difficult and error-prone. Programming languages were developed to give programmers a more human-readable way to express instructions.

Low-level languages are close to the hardware. They offer fine control over exactly how the processor operates, but they are difficult to read, write, and maintain. High-level languages use English-like syntax, hide the complexity of the hardware, and can run on many different types of processor without modification.

Key Fact

High-level languages are easier to write and debug, portable across hardware, and closer to natural language. Low-level languages give precise hardware control and can produce faster, more efficient code, but they are harder to write and specific to one processor type.

Machine Code and Assembly Language

Machine code is the only language a processor can execute directly. It is expressed entirely in binary and is specific to a processor or family of processors — code written for one architecture will not run on a different one without modification.

Assembly language replaces raw binary with short, memorable codes called mnemonics (for example, MOV to move data, ADD to add two values). Each line of assembly corresponds to exactly one machine code instruction — this is called a 1:1 correspondence. Assembly language is still tightly bound to the processor’s architecture and is most commonly used when developing software for embedded systems or when direct control over specific hardware is needed.

Translators: Compiler, Interpreter, Assembler

Because processors only understand machine code, any program written in a high-level or assembly language must be translated before it can run. There are three types of translator: the compiler, the interpreter, and the assembler.

A compiler reads the entire source code of a program and translates it all into machine code at once. The output is an executable file that can be run as many times as needed without the compiler being present. Errors are only reported after the whole program has been analysed, which makes them easier to review together. Once compiled, the program runs quickly because no further translation is needed at run time.

An interpreter translates and executes a program one line at a time. It does not produce a standalone machine code file; instead, it calls appropriate machine code subroutines within its own code to carry out each statement. If the program encounters an error mid-way, it stops at that line — making it easier to spot exactly where a mistake occurred. The downside is that the interpreter must be present every time the program runs, and execution is generally slower because translation happens at run time.

An assembler converts assembly language into machine code. Because each assembly mnemonic maps directly to one machine code instruction (the 1:1 correspondence), this translation is straightforward. Like a compiler, an assembler translates its input into machine code directly — the output is machine code that the processor can execute.

Key distinction for your exam: both assemblers and compilers translate their input directly into machine code. Interpreters do not generate machine code directly — they call machine code subroutines to carry out each statement.

Most modern high-level languages are typically run using an interpreter during development (easier debugging, immediate feedback) and compiled for the final product (faster execution, no dependency on the interpreter). Some languages use a combination of both approaches, compiling to an intermediate form before interpreting.

networks-cyber-security.title: Networks, Network Types and Protocols
networks-cyber-security.description: PAN, LAN and WAN, wired vs wireless trade-offs, and the protocols that make the internet work.
networks-cyber-security.content_html:
What Is a Computer Network?

A computer network is two or more devices linked so they can exchange data and share resources. Networks range from two laptops connected at home to millions of devices spanning the globe. Without networks, every device would be an island: no email, no streaming, no online banking, no shared printing in a school.

Networks offer significant advantages: files can be shared between users without physical media, a single internet connection can be shared across many devices, centralised storage makes backups easier, and users can communicate in real time. The disadvantages include the cost of setting up and maintaining the hardware, the risk of spreading malware across connected devices, and the need for security measures to protect shared data.

Key Fact

The three main network types are: PAN (Personal Area Network) — a very short-range network between personal devices, typically using Bluetooth; LAN (Local Area Network) — covers a small area such as a school or office and is usually owned by one organisation; WAN (Wide Area Network) — covers a large geographic area and is typically under collective or distributed ownership.

PAN, LAN and WAN

A PAN (Personal Area Network) connects devices within the range of a single person, typically up to about ten metres. Bluetooth is the technology you need to know for PANs: it connects a smartphone to wireless earbuds, a laptop to a wireless keyboard, or a smartwatch to a phone. PANs are low-cost and require no infrastructure, but they are only suitable for personal device pairing, not for sharing resources across an organisation.

A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a relatively small area — a school, a hospital ward, an office floor. The hardware (cables, switches, routers) is usually owned and managed by the organisation itself. LANs typically offer high-speed connections because devices are physically close together and the network infrastructure is dedicated to that organisation.

A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a wide geographic area, connecting multiple LANs across cities, countries, or continents. WANs rely on third-party telecommunications infrastructure — leased telephone lines, undersea cables, or satellite links — meaning no single organisation owns the whole network. The internet is the largest example of a WAN.

LANs cover a small area; WANs cover a large area. LANs are typically owned by one organisation; WANs use infrastructure owned by multiple parties. LANs tend to offer higher speeds and lower latency because devices are physically close; WAN speeds vary and depend on the quality of telecommunications links between sites. Setting up a LAN is relatively low-cost; connecting to a WAN typically involves paying for leased lines or internet service provider fees. Both can use wired or wireless technology.

Wired vs Wireless Networks

Wired networks use physical cables. Fibre optic cable carries data as pulses of light and can achieve very high speeds over long distances with minimal signal degradation — it is used for backbone connections between buildings and for connecting homes to the internet. Copper cable (such as twisted-pair Ethernet cable) is cheaper and easier to install, but its speed and range are more limited and it is more susceptible to electrical interference.

Wireless networks transmit data using radio waves. The main advantage is mobility: devices can connect from anywhere within range without needing a physical cable. This makes wireless ideal for laptops, tablets and smartphones. However, wireless connections are generally slower and less reliable than wired equivalents, more susceptible to interference from walls and other devices, and potentially less secure because any device within range can attempt to connect. Wireless signals can also be degraded by distance from the access point.

Network Protocols

A network protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication. Without protocols, devices from different manufacturers using different operating systems could not exchange data reliably. Protocols define how data is formatted, addressed, transmitted, and error-checked.

Key Fact

The protocols you must know: IP (addresses and routes data packets across networks), TCP (sets up the connection and ensures reliable delivery), HTTP (transfers web pages), HTTPS (encrypted web transfer), SMTP (sends emails), IMAP (receives and manages emails on a mail server).

IP (Internet Protocol) — assigns a unique address to every device on the internet and handles the addressing and routing of data packets. When data is sent across the internet, IP ensures each packet is labelled with the source and destination address so routers can forward it along the correct path.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — works with IP to set up a reliable connection between two devices. TCP breaks data into packets, numbers them, and checks that all packets arrive and are reassembled correctly. If a packet is lost, TCP requests it to be sent again.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — defines how web browsers and web servers exchange web pages. When you type a website address, your browser sends an HTTP request; the server responds with the page content.

HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) — an encrypted version of HTTP. The data exchanged between browser and server is scrambled so it cannot be read if intercepted. Essential for banking, shopping and login pages.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — used to send emails from a client to a mail server, and between mail servers. When you press Send, your email application uses SMTP.

IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) — allows an email client to access and manage email stored on a remote mail server. Emails remain on the server and are synchronised across all devices. This is important: note that POP3 is not on the required protocol list for this specification — IMAP is the email-receiving protocol to know.

networks-cyber-security.title: Network Security and the TCP/IP Model
networks-cyber-security.description: Authentication, encryption, firewalls, MAC filtering and how the four-layer TCP/IP model organises traffic.
networks-cyber-security.content_html:
Why Network Security Matters

Every device connected to a network is a potential target. A school network holds thousands of student records; a hospital network carries patient data; a retail network processes payment details. Network security refers to the combination of measures used to protect these systems. No single measure is perfect, so effective security uses multiple layers working together.

Key Fact

The four network security methods you must know are: authentication (verifying who a user is), encryption (scrambling data so it cannot be read if intercepted), firewalls (monitoring and filtering network traffic), and MAC address filtering (allowing or blocking devices based on their hardware address).

Authentication

Authentication is the first line of defence. Before a user can access a network, the system must confirm who they are. The simplest form is a username and password: the username identifies the user, and the password proves it is really them. Stronger authentication uses multiple factors — for example, a password combined with a one-time code sent to a mobile phone (two-factor authentication). Authentication ensures that only authorised users can access resources, even if an attacker knows the network exists.

Encryption

Encryption protects data in transit and in storage. When data is encrypted, it is transformed into ciphertext — an unreadable scramble of characters. Only someone with the correct decryption key can restore it to its original form. On networks, encryption is used by HTTPS (which encrypts web traffic between a browser and a server) and by secure email systems. Even if an attacker intercepts encrypted data travelling across a network, they cannot read it without the key.

Firewalls

A firewall acts as a gatekeeper between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external network such as the internet. It examines each packet of data and decides whether to allow it through or block it, based on predefined rules. For example, a school might configure its firewall to block traffic to certain categories of website, or to block all incoming connections on ports not needed for school systems. Firewalls can be hardware devices, software running on a computer, or a combination of both.

MAC Address Filtering

Every network interface card (NIC) has a unique MAC address (Media Access Control address) assigned by its manufacturer. MAC address filtering uses this address to control which devices can connect to a network. A network administrator creates a list of approved MAC addresses; only devices on the list can access the network. This is useful for restricting access to a wireless network in a school, preventing unauthorised devices from connecting even if they know the Wi-Fi password. A limitation is that MAC addresses can be changed in software (called MAC spoofing), so it should not be relied upon as the sole security measure.

A well-secured network layers its defences. Authentication prevents unauthorised users from logging in. MAC address filtering prevents unauthorised devices from connecting. A firewall blocks suspicious traffic that does reach the network. Encryption protects data even if it is intercepted in transit. Each layer compensates for the weaknesses of the others. For example, a firewall cannot protect against an attacker who already has valid credentials — but authentication can. Together, they provide a much stronger defence than any single measure alone.

The Four-Layer TCP/IP Model

When data travels across a network, the process is organised into four distinct layers. Each layer handles a specific job, and data passes through all four layers on its way from sender to receiver. This is the TCP/IP model, named after its two key protocols. Using layers means each component can be developed and updated independently: a new application protocol can be added without changing how packets are routed.

Key Fact

The four layers of the TCP/IP model, from top to bottom: Application (where network applications operate — HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP), Transport (sets up communication and manages packets — TCP), Internet (addressing and routing packets — IP), Link (network hardware and drivers — NIC, OS device drivers).

Application layer — this is where network applications operate. Web browsers, email clients, and file transfer tools all sit at this layer. The protocols at this layer — HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, and IMAP — define how those applications format and exchange data.

Transport layer — sets up the communication session between two hosts and agrees settings such as the size of data packets. TCP operates at this layer, providing reliable, ordered delivery by breaking data into packets, numbering them, and checking they all arrive correctly. If a packet is lost, TCP requests it again.

Internet layer — handles addressing and routing. IP operates at this layer: it assigns a source and destination IP address to each packet and determines the best path through the network of routers to reach the destination.

Link layer — the lowest layer, responsible for the physical transmission of data across a single link. The network interface card (NIC) sits here, along with the operating system’s device drivers that communicate with it. This layer handles the actual electrical or optical signals on the cable or wireless channel.

When data is sent, it passes down through the layers on the sender’s device (Application → Transport → Internet → Link), crosses the network physically, and then passes up through the layers on the receiver’s device (Link → Internet → Transport → Application) to be reassembled and delivered to the application.

networks-cyber-security.title: Cyber Security Threats and Social Engineering
networks-cyber-security.description: Malware, social engineering tactics, weak passwords and unpatched software, plus penetration testing.
networks-cyber-security.content_html:
What Is Cyber Security?

Cyber security is the field concerned with defending digital systems and data. It matters to everyone: a UK bank holding millions of customer accounts, a school storing pupil data, a teenager with a social media profile. Cyber threats do not require physical proximity — an attacker can target a system from anywhere in the world, which is what makes them so difficult to defend against.

Threats come from multiple directions. Some exploit technical weaknesses in software or networks. Others exploit the most unpredictable component of any system: the people using it. Understanding how attacks work is the first step towards defending against them.

Social Engineering

Social engineering targets human psychology rather than technical flaws. Attackers create believable scenarios to trick people into doing something they would not normally do — revealing a password, clicking a link, or unlocking a door. The three forms you need to know are blagging, phishing, and shouldering.

Key Fact

The three social engineering techniques: blagging (pretexting) — creating a fabricated scenario to trick a victim into revealing information; phishing — using fraudulent emails or messages to obtain private information; shouldering — observing someone’s private information over their shoulder, such as watching a PIN being entered at a cashpoint.

Blagging (pretexting) involves inventing a convincing story. An attacker might call a company helpdesk pretending to be an IT contractor who urgently needs a user’s login reset, or claim to be a bank employee asking a customer to “verify” their account details. The invented scenario is designed to create a sense of urgency or authority that overrides the target’s normal caution.

Phishing typically arrives as an email or text message that appears to come from a trusted source — a bank, a delivery company, or a well-known retailer. The message creates urgency (“Your account will be suspended”) and directs the target to a fake website designed to harvest their login credentials. Spear phishing is a targeted form aimed at a specific individual, making the deception more convincing.

Shouldering (shoulder surfing) is the simplest form of social engineering: physically watching someone enter private information. It happens at cashpoints, on public transport when someone reads emails over a stranger’s shoulder, or in an office when someone watches a colleague type a password.

Malware

Malware (malicious software) covers a range of programs designed to cause harm. The three types specified for this course are: computer viruses, trojans, and spyware.

A computer virus attaches itself to an existing file or program. When the infected file is opened or shared, the virus copies itself to other files. Viruses require a host file and rely on user action to spread — for example, opening an infected email attachment or copying a file from an infected USB drive.

A trojan (sometimes called a trojan horse) disguises itself as useful software — a free game, a codec, an update. Once installed, it operates silently in the background. Unlike a virus, a trojan does not self-replicate; instead, it typically opens a back door that allows an attacker to access the infected system remotely.

Spyware runs hidden in the background and monitors the user’s activity. A keylogger is a common form: it records every key pressed, capturing passwords, bank details, and messages. The data is transmitted back to the attacker without the user knowing the software is even present.

Other Threats

Pharming redirects users to a fake website without them clicking any suspicious link. Unlike phishing (which relies on deceiving the user into clicking), pharming tampers with the underlying address resolution process — so even typing a correct bank web address into a browser might lead to a fake copy of that site.

Several other conditions create vulnerabilities. Weak and default passwords are easily guessed or cracked: using “password”, “admin”, or a device’s factory-set password leaves an obvious entry point. Misconfigured access rights occur when users have more permissions than their role requires — for example, a data entry clerk with admin rights could accidentally or deliberately delete critical records. Removable media (USB drives, external disks) can introduce malware when plugged into a device, either deliberately or because the drive was infected elsewhere. Unpatched or outdated software contains known security vulnerabilities that developers have since fixed in updates — systems running old software are exposed to attacks that exploit those known weaknesses.

Penetration Testing

Penetration testing is a defensive technique: organisations hire specialist testers to attack their own systems legally and intentionally. The goal is to discover weaknesses before a malicious attacker does. There are two key approaches:

Key Fact

Two types of penetration test: internal (white-box) — the tester has knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials, simulating a malicious insider such as a rogue employee; external (black-box) — the tester has no knowledge of the system or credentials, simulating an outside attacker with no prior access.

networks-cyber-security.title: Detecting and Preventing Cyber Threats
networks-cyber-security.description: Biometrics, password systems, CAPTCHA, email confirmation and automatic updates as defences.
networks-cyber-security.content_html:
Defence in Depth

No single security measure can stop every attack. The most effective approach is layered defence: stacking multiple measures so that if one fails, another is still in place. This lesson covers the five specific prevention measures from the specification: biometric measures, password systems, CAPTCHA, email confirmation, and automatic software updates. Understanding what each one does — and crucially, what it is protecting against — is more useful than simply memorising definitions.

Key Fact

The five security measures to know: biometric measures (authenticating by physical characteristics), password systems (verifying identity by secret credentials), CAPTCHA (distinguishing humans from automated bots), email confirmation (verifying a user’s identity or an action via their email account), and automatic software updates (patching known vulnerabilities as soon as fixes are available).

Biometric Measures

Biometric measures authenticate users using unique physical characteristics. Common examples include fingerprint scanning, facial recognition, and iris scanning. These are particularly common on mobile devices: a smartphone’s fingerprint sensor or face unlock feature uses biometric data stored securely on the device to confirm that the person picking up the phone is its owner.

Biometrics offer a significant advantage over passwords: a fingerprint cannot be forgotten and is very difficult for another person to replicate. However, biometric data is permanent — unlike a password, you cannot change your fingerprints if they are ever compromised. This is why biometric data is usually combined with another factor rather than used alone.

Password Systems

A password system is the most widely used form of authentication. A strong password is long, contains a mix of letters, numbers and symbols, and is not based on easily guessed information such as a name or date of birth. Weak or default passwords are a major vulnerability: attackers use automated tools to systematically try common passwords (a dictionary attack) or all possible combinations (a brute-force attack).

Password systems become significantly stronger when combined with a second factor. Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires the user to provide something they know (the password) and something they have (such as a one-time code sent to their phone). Even if an attacker obtains the password, they cannot log in without also having access to the second factor.

Length matters more than complexity. A short, complex password like X7!q is cracked far faster by brute force than a long passphrase like PurpleElephantRunsFast, because the number of possible combinations grows exponentially with each additional character. A strong password should be at least 12 characters long, mix upper and lower case with numbers and symbols, not be a dictionary word or a predictable modification of one, and be unique to each account (reusing passwords means that if one site is breached, all accounts sharing that password are at risk).

CAPTCHA

CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. It is the tick-box, image-selection, or distorted-text puzzle you encounter when logging in or creating an account online. Its purpose is to block automated bots from performing actions at scale — such as creating thousands of fake accounts, submitting spam through a contact form, or attempting to brute-force a login by trying thousands of password combinations rapidly.

CAPTCHA exploits the fact that certain tasks which are trivial for a human brain (identifying traffic lights in a photograph, reading slightly skewed letters) are computationally difficult for automated programs. By requiring users to complete these challenges, websites ensure that an actual human is behind the keyboard. Modern versions use behavioural analysis to assess whether a user interacts with a page in a human-like way, making them more seamless for genuine users while still blocking bots.

Email Confirmation

Email confirmation uses a person’s email account as a secondary verification channel. When a user creates a new account, the site sends a confirmation link to their email address; the account is only activated when the link is clicked. This proves the person registering actually has access to that email address — a bot or an attacker using a fake email address will not be able to complete the confirmation step.

Email confirmation is also used when security-sensitive actions are requested: resetting a password, changing an email address, or authorising a large bank transfer. Sending a one-time link or code to the registered email means an attacker who only knows a password cannot complete the action without also having access to the email inbox.

Key Fact

Biometrics work best on personal devices where a physical characteristic is available. Passwords are universal but weakest when short or reused. CAPTCHA stops automated bot attacks. Email confirmation proves both ownership of an email address and intent to perform an action. Automatic updates close known software vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. Used together, these measures create a much harder target.

Automatic Software Updates

Automatic software updates address one of the most exploited vulnerabilities in any system: outdated software. Software contains flaws — bugs in its code that, when discovered by attackers, can be exploited to gain unauthorised access, install malware, or crash a system. When a vulnerability is found, developers release a patch (a targeted fix). Unpatched software is exposed to attacks specifically designed to target that known flaw.

Enabling automatic updates means patches are applied as soon as they become available, minimising the window of vulnerability. Manually updating systems is unreliable — users often delay or ignore update prompts. Automatic updates are particularly important for operating systems and security software such as anti-malware tools, which need to know about the latest threats to protect against them.

Consider a banking app on a smartphone. To protect the account, the bank applies several layers: the phone uses biometrics (face or fingerprint) to prevent strangers using the device; a strong password or PIN is required to log in; a CAPTCHA stops automated login attempts; when logging in from a new device, an email confirmation is sent; and the app updates automatically to patch security vulnerabilities. An attacker who defeats one layer still faces the others. Removing any single layer increases risk — but no single layer is the whole defence.

databases-sql.title: Relational Databases: Tables, Keys and Relationships
databases-sql.description: Tables, records, fields, primary keys and foreign keys — why relations beat one big spreadsheet.
databases-sql.content_html:
What Is a Database?

A database is an organised collection of data. Unlike a simple spreadsheet, a database is designed to store large amounts of information and allow it to be searched, sorted and updated quickly. Schools use databases to store pupil records; hospitals use them to track patient appointments; online shops use them to manage product stock. Anywhere large amounts of structured data need to be managed, a database is the tool of choice.

Relational Databases

A relational database stores data in multiple linked tables rather than one large list. Each table holds data about a single topic (for example, students, or courses). The tables are connected to each other using special key fields. This structure was developed to solve two serious problems that arise when you try to keep everything in one place: data redundancy and data inconsistency.

Key Fact

Data redundancy means storing the same piece of data in more than one place. Data inconsistency means different copies of the same data ending up with different values. Relational databases tackle both by storing each piece of data in exactly one place.

Tables, Records and Fields

Every relational database is made up of tables. Each table has a name (for example, Students) and is divided into columns called fields (or attributes) and rows called records (or tuples).

  • A field (also called an attribute) is a single category of data — for example, student_name or year_group. Each field has a specified data type: text, integer, date, Boolean and so on.
  • A record (also called a tuple or row) is one complete entry in the table — all the data about one particular student, for example.

Think of a table like a grid: the column headings are the fields, and each row is a record. Here is a sample Students table:

The Students table has four fields: student_id, student_name, year_group, tutor_group.

Sample records:

1 | Aisha Khan | 10 | 10A
2 | Ben Okafor | 11 | 11B
3 | Chloe Davis | 10 | 10A

Here student_id is the primary key — each student has a unique number that is never repeated or reused. The other fields store descriptive information about the student. Notice that 10A appears twice: this is fine because it is just a tutor group label, not the student’s main identifier.

Primary Keys

Every table must have a primary key. This is a field whose value is different for every record, so it can be used to pinpoint exactly one row. In the Students table, student_id is the primary key. You cannot use student_name as a primary key because two students could share the same name.

Primary keys are often auto-generated integers (1, 2, 3…) although they can be any unique value — an NHS number, a National Insurance number, a barcode. The key point is that no two records can ever have the same primary key value, and the field must always have a value (it cannot be left blank).

Foreign Keys

A second table—say, an Enrolments table—needs to know which student each enrolment belongs to. Rather than copy the student’s full name and year group into the Enrolments table (which would create redundancy), we store only the student’s student_id. In the Enrolments table, this field is called a foreign key.

The foreign key “points to” the primary key in the other table. This is how the two tables are linked. If you want to find a student’s name for a given enrolment, you look up the student_id in the Students table using the foreign key as a reference.

We have two tables:

Students (student_id [PK], student_name, year_group)
Courses (course_id [PK], course_title)
Enrolments (enrolment_id [PK], student_id [FK], course_id [FK])

The Enrolments table uses student_id as a foreign key linking back to Students, and course_id as a foreign key linking back to Courses. This means:

  • Aisha’s name is stored once in Students — there is no need to write “Aisha Khan” in every enrolment row for her.
  • If Aisha’s name is ever corrected, you update it in one place and it is immediately correct everywhere — no inconsistency possible.

Relationships Between Tables

The most common relationship at GCSE is a one-to-many relationship. In our example, one student can have many enrolments, but each enrolment belongs to exactly one student. The foreign key always sits in the “many” side of the relationship (the Enrolments table), pointing back to the primary key on the “one” side (the Students table).

Key Fact

A primary key uniquely identifies a record in its own table. A foreign key in one table references the primary key in another table, linking the two tables together. In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key is always in the “many” table.

Why Not Just Use One Big Table?

Imagine trying to store all student and course information in a single flat table with columns like: student_id, student_name, year_group, course_title, teacher_name, room_number. Every time a student takes two courses, you would need two rows — with the student’s name and year group repeated in both. This is data redundancy. Now imagine the student changes year group: you would need to update every row for that student. Miss one, and you now have inconsistent data. The relational approach solves both problems by splitting data across properly linked tables.

Vocabulary Equivalence Note

The same concepts appear with different names depending on context. When discussing an abstract data model: an entity maps to a table; an attribute maps to a field; an entity identifier maps to a primary key. Your exam may use either set of terms — you need to recognise both.

databases-sql.title: SQL: Retrieving Data with SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY
databases-sql.description: Writing SQL queries to retrieve data, filter with WHERE conditions and sort results with ORDER BY.
databases-sql.content_html:
What Is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to communicate with a relational database. When a website shows you a list of products, when a teacher pulls up your grades, or when a bank checks your balance, SQL is running behind the scenes. In this lesson, we focus on retrieving data — asking the database to show us records that match certain criteria.

We will use the same three tables introduced in the previous lesson throughout all our examples:

  • Students — student_id (PK), student_name, year_group
  • Courses — course_id (PK), course_title
  • Enrolments — enrolment_id (PK), student_id (FK), course_id (FK)

SELECT and FROM

Every retrieval query begins with SELECT, followed by the column names you want to see. Then comes FROM, followed by the table name. If you want all columns, use a star (*) instead of listing them.

Query: Show all data from the Students table.

SELECT *
FROM Students;

The * means “all columns”. The database returns every row and every field from the Students table. The semicolon marks the end of the query.

Query: Show only the student_name column from the Students table.

SELECT student_name
FROM Students;

This time only one column is returned. You can list multiple columns separated by commas: SELECT student_name, year_group FROM Students;

Filtering with WHERE

Most of the time you don’t want every row — you want rows that meet a condition. The WHERE clause lets you set that condition. The database checks each row and only includes it in the results if the condition is true.

You can use these comparison operators in a WHERE clause: = (equal), <> (not equal), < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal to), >= (greater than or equal to). You can also combine conditions with AND and OR, and use LIKE with a % wildcard for partial text matches.

Equal to (text value):

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE student_name = ‘Aisha Khan’;

Text values are wrapped in single quotes. This returns only the row where the student’s name is exactly ‘Aisha Khan’.

Greater than (numeric value):

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE year_group > 10;

Returns only students in year 11 (or above, if higher year groups exist). Numbers do not need quotes.

Combining conditions with AND:

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE year_group = 10 AND student_name LIKE ‘A%’;

Both conditions must be true. LIKE ‘A%’ matches any name that starts with the letter A. The % is a wildcard meaning “any characters here”.

Either condition with OR:

SELECT *
FROM Students
WHERE year_group = 10 OR year_group = 11;

Returns students in year 10 OR year 11 — either condition being true is enough to include the row.

Key Fact

In a WHERE clause: text values go inside single quotes; numbers do not. The wildcard character % is used with LIKE: LIKE ‘%son’ matches anything ending in ‘son’; LIKE ‘A%’ matches anything starting with ‘A’; LIKE ‘%art%’ matches anything containing ‘art’.

Sorting with ORDER BY

By default, rows come back in no guaranteed order. To sort the results, add an ORDER BY clause at the end of the query, followed by the column name. Use ASC for ascending order (A to Z, lowest to highest) or DESC for descending order (Z to A, highest to lowest). If you leave out ASC or DESC, the database defaults to ascending.

Alphabetical order:

SELECT student_name
FROM Students
ORDER BY student_name ASC;

Returns all student names sorted A to Z.

Filtered and sorted together:

SELECT student_name, year_group
FROM Students
WHERE year_group = 10
ORDER BY student_name DESC;

Returns only year 10 students, but sorted Z to A by name. Notice the clause order: SELECT — FROM — WHERE — ORDER BY. This order is fixed and must not be changed.

Querying Across Two Tables

Exam questions may ask you to retrieve data from two tables at once. You can do this by listing both tables after FROM and adding a WHERE condition that matches the primary key in one table to the foreign key in the other. This effectively joins the tables by finding rows where the key values match.

Task: Find the names of all students enrolled on course number 3.

SELECT Students.student_name
FROM Students, Enrolments
WHERE Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id
AND Enrolments.course_id = 3;

Step by step: FROM Students, Enrolments tells the database to look at both tables. WHERE Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id links the two tables through matching key values (primary key = foreign key). The second AND condition filters to course 3 only. You can use TableName.ColumnName notation when the same column name appears in both tables, to avoid ambiguity.

Key Fact

The four retrieval keywords must appear in this order: SELECT (what columns) → FROM (which table or tables) → WHERE (which rows, optional) → ORDER BY (what sort order, optional). Swapping the order causes a syntax error.

databases-sql.title: SQL: Modifying Data with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
databases-sql.description: Using INSERT INTO to add rows, UPDATE SET to modify data, and DELETE FROM with a safe WHERE clause.
databases-sql.content_html:
Modifying a Database

So far you have learnt to retrieve data with SELECT. Real databases also need to grow and change: new students join a school and need rows adding; contact details change and need updating; leavers’ records are eventually removed. SQL provides three commands for these operations: INSERT INTO, UPDATE, and DELETE FROM. We use the same Students, Courses and Enrolments tables as before throughout all the examples in this lesson.

Reminder of the schema:
Students — student_id (PK), student_name, year_group
Courses — course_id (PK), course_title
Enrolments — enrolment_id (PK), student_id (FK), course_id (FK)

INSERT INTO — Adding New Rows

To add a new record, use:

INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, …)
VALUES (value1, value2, …);

The columns list and the values list must match in number and order. Text values go in single quotes; integers do not. You do not have to include every column — you can omit columns that have a default value or are auto-generated by the database (such as an auto-increment primary key).

Task: Add a new student, Dani Osei, in year group 10, with student_id 4.

INSERT INTO Students (student_id, student_name, year_group)
VALUES (4, ‘Dani Osei’, 10);

After this query runs, the Students table gains a new row: 4 | Dani Osei | 10. Notice that 4 (an integer) has no quotes, while ‘Dani Osei’ (text) does.

Adding an enrolment record: To enrol Dani (student_id = 4) on course 2:

INSERT INTO Enrolments (enrolment_id, student_id, course_id)
VALUES (10, 4, 2);

All three values are integers so none need quotes. The foreign key value (student_id = 4) must already exist in the Students table — you cannot enrol a student who doesn’t exist.

UPDATE — Changing Existing Data

To change data in existing rows, use:

UPDATE table_name
SET column1 = value1, column2 = value2, …
WHERE condition;

The SET clause names the columns to change and their new values. The WHERE clause identifies which rows to update. You can update more than one column at once by separating them with commas in the SET clause.

Task: Change Aisha Khan’s year group to 11.

UPDATE Students
SET year_group = 11
WHERE student_name = ‘Aisha Khan’;

Only the row (or rows) where student_name equals ‘Aisha Khan’ is changed. All other rows remain exactly as they were.

Updating two columns at once: Rename student_id 2 and move them to year 11.

UPDATE Students
SET student_name = ‘Benjamin Okafor’, year_group = 11
WHERE student_id = 2;

Two columns are updated in a single query. Using student_id in the WHERE clause is safer than using student_name, because student_id is the primary key and uniquely identifies one row.

Key Fact

Critical rule: An UPDATE without a WHERE clause changes every single row in the table. Writing UPDATE Students SET year_group = 11; would change all students’ year groups to 11, overwriting all existing data. Always include a WHERE clause to target only the intended rows.

DELETE FROM — Removing Rows

To remove one or more rows from a table, use:

DELETE FROM table_name
WHERE condition;

The WHERE clause identifies which rows to remove. Every row matching the condition is permanently deleted — this cannot be undone in a basic SQL query. If no WHERE clause is given, every row in the table is deleted.

Task: Remove the student with student_id 3 from the Students table.

DELETE FROM Students
WHERE student_id = 3;

Only the row where student_id = 3 is deleted. Using the primary key in the WHERE clause ensures exactly one row is targeted.

Deleting an enrolment: Remove all enrolments for student_id 1.

DELETE FROM Enrolments
WHERE student_id = 1;

If student 1 has three enrolment records, all three are deleted by this single query because all three rows satisfy the condition.

Key Fact

The WHERE clause on DELETE is never optional in practice. DELETE FROM Students; without a WHERE clause deletes every student record in the table — all data is lost. Always test a WHERE condition with a SELECT query first to confirm it targets the right rows, before running DELETE.

Test Before You Modify

A good habit before running any UPDATE or DELETE on a real database is to first run a SELECT query with the same WHERE condition. If the SELECT returns exactly the rows you expected, you can be confident the UPDATE or DELETE will target the right records and no others. For example, before running DELETE FROM Students WHERE year_group = 10; first run SELECT * FROM Students WHERE year_group = 10; to review exactly which rows will be affected. This test-first approach is a practical way to prevent accidental data loss.

Comparing the Three Commands

To summarise the three data-modification commands:

  • INSERT INTO — adds one new row. Needs column names and matching values. Cannot target existing rows.
  • UPDATE…SET…WHERE — changes values in existing rows. Must use WHERE to target specific rows. Can update multiple columns in one query.
  • DELETE FROM…WHERE — removes whole rows. Must use WHERE to target specific rows. The deletion is immediate and permanent.

ethical-legal-environmental.title: Ethical and Legal Issues in Digital Technology
ethical-legal-environmental.description: Privacy, hacking, cloud storage, wearable tech and the UK laws that protect users and creators.
ethical-legal-environmental.content_html:
Why Technology Raises Ethical Questions

Digital technology has transformed how we communicate, shop, access healthcare and use public services. But with those benefits come serious questions: who controls your personal data, what happens when someone accesses a computer without permission, and who owns the software or music you stream? Ethical issues are questions about right and wrong that often have no single correct answer. Legal issues are those that the law defines as permitted or prohibited.

Privacy and Personal Data

Privacy is one of the central ethical concerns of the digital age. Every time you use a smartphone, search engine, social media platform or banking app, data about you is collected. This data may include your location, browsing history, financial transactions, health metrics and social connections. Most people value the ability to control what others know about them, and many feel uncomfortable when they discover how much data organisations hold.

New technologies intensify this challenge:

  • Mobile technologies — smartphones carry GPS sensors, cameras and microphones that can record location and activity continuously. Apps often request permissions to access these sensors beyond what is strictly necessary for the app to function.
  • Wireless networking — public Wi-Fi hotspots can be monitored; poorly secured home routers can expose household devices. Data transmitted without encryption can be intercepted.
  • Cloud storage — saving files to a cloud service means a third-party company holds copies of your data on remote servers. Questions arise about who can access those files and what the provider does with your metadata.
  • Wearable technologies — fitness trackers, smartwatches and medical monitoring devices collect continuous biometric data such as heart rate, sleep patterns and physical activity. This data is highly personal and could affect insurance premiums or employment decisions if shared inappropriately.
  • Computer-based implants — devices implanted in the body (such as pacemakers or neural interfaces) raise profound ethical questions about bodily autonomy, data security and the consequences of a security breach on a person’s health.
Key Fact

Technologies explicitly named in this topic include: mobile technologies, wireless networking, cloud storage, wearable technologies, computer-based implants and autonomous vehicles. For each, you should be able to describe at least one ethical or privacy concern and one benefit.

Hacking and Unauthorised Access

Hacking is the act of gaining access to a computer system without permission. This may involve exploiting security vulnerabilities, using stolen passwords or writing malicious software. Hacking can result in theft of personal data, financial fraud, disruption of services (such as hospital systems going offline) and reputational damage to organisations. Ethically, even “white hat” security researchers who probe systems to find weaknesses must operate within defined legal agreements — probing a system without permission is illegal regardless of intent.

Government Access vs. Citizen Privacy

One of the most debated ethical dilemmas is whether governments and security services should be able to access citizens’ private data. Most people value their privacy and are uncomfortable with the idea of their messages being read or their locations tracked by the state. However, governments and security agencies argue that access to private communications is sometimes necessary to prevent terrorism, serious crime and national security threats. There is genuine tension here, with no universally agreed answer: stronger government surveillance may prevent attacks but also risks misuse of that power and chilling effects on free speech.

Arguments for greater government access: Security services may need to monitor communications to identify terrorist plots before they occur. Without access to encrypted messages, criminals can organise undetected. Proponents argue that citizens with nothing to hide have nothing to fear.

Arguments against: Mass surveillance undermines the presumption of innocence. Governments could misuse data to target political opponents or journalists. Mandatory encryption backdoors would weaken security for everyone, including ordinary users and businesses, since the same backdoor that governments use could also be exploited by criminal hackers.

UK Legal Frameworks

Three key Acts of Parliament govern the legal use of technology in the UK. These are not optional guidelines — breaking them can result in fines, civil claims or criminal prosecution.

The Data Protection Act 2018 governs how organisations handle personal data. It incorporates the requirements of the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR). Organisations must collect data only for a specific, stated purpose; keep it secure; not hold it longer than necessary; and give individuals the right to see, correct or request deletion of their own data. Failure to comply can result in significant fines issued by the Information Commissioner’s Office. This Act replaced the earlier Data Protection Act 1998.

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it a criminal offence to access a computer system without authorisation. It covers three categories of offence: unauthorised access to computer material (for example, logging into someone else’s account); unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences (for example, accessing a bank’s server to commit fraud); and unauthorised modification of computer material (for example, installing malware or deleting data). A 2015 amendment to the Act increased maximum penalties and added offences relating to attacks on computer infrastructure.

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects intellectual property. Software, music, images, films and written work are automatically protected from the moment of creation. Copying, distributing or publicly performing copyrighted material without permission — whether commercial or personal — is illegal. This is why downloading music or films through unauthorised channels is not just unethical but against the law.

Key Fact

Three UK laws you must know: Data Protection Act 2018 — controls personal data handling; Computer Misuse Act 1990 — makes hacking and malware creation criminal offences; Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 — protects software, music and other creative works from unauthorised copying.

ethical-legal-environmental.title: Autonomous Vehicles and Environmental Impacts
ethical-legal-environmental.description: Self-driving car ethics, data centre energy use, e-waste and balancing digital benefit against harm.
ethical-legal-environmental.content_html:
Autonomous Vehicles

An autonomous vehicle is a vehicle that can drive itself, using sensors (cameras, radar, lidar), artificial intelligence and real-time mapping to navigate roads without a human at the controls. Partially autonomous features — such as lane-keeping assistance, automatic braking and motorway cruise control — are already widely available. Fully self-driving taxis and freight lorries are being tested in several countries. The potential benefits are significant: reduced road accidents caused by human error, improved mobility for people who cannot drive, smoother traffic flow, and reduced need for parking in cities.

Ethical Challenges of Self-Driving Cars

Autonomous vehicles raise ethical questions that have no easy answers. These questions are sometimes framed around thought experiments involving unavoidable collision scenarios: if an autonomous vehicle cannot stop in time, should its algorithm prioritise the passenger, a pedestrian, or act in a way that minimises total harm? No consensus has emerged on how these algorithms should be programmed, and different cultural attitudes produce different intuitions.

Decision-making algorithms: When a collision is unavoidable, who or what should the vehicle’s programming prioritise? Choosing the passenger’s safety above others seems self-serving; choosing to minimise total harm treats the passenger as expendable. These decisions are currently made by engineers and, ultimately, by manufacturers — raising questions of accountability and transparency.

Liability after collisions: With a human driver, blame is relatively straightforward to assign. With an autonomous vehicle, responsibility may lie with the vehicle manufacturer, the software developer, the road authority, the person who set the destination, or some combination of all of these. Current legal frameworks are not well-equipped to deal with this complexity.

Displacement of workers: Large-scale adoption of autonomous vehicles would affect millions of people employed as taxi drivers, lorry drivers, bus drivers and delivery workers. The technology could improve safety and efficiency, but at a significant social cost to those workers and the communities that depend on those jobs. Retraining and social support would be needed at scale.

Security and hacking: An autonomous vehicle is essentially a computer on wheels. If its systems were hacked, a vehicle could be manipulated remotely — creating a physical safety risk as well as a digital security risk.

Key Fact

Three core ethical issues with autonomous vehicles: decision-making algorithms (who is prioritised in unavoidable accidents?), liability (who is legally responsible when an autonomous vehicle is involved in a collision?), and job displacement (what happens to millions of professional drivers?).

Environmental Impacts of Digital Technology

Digital technology is often described as “clean” compared with heavy industry, but its environmental footprint is substantial. There are three main categories of environmental impact: manufacturing, energy consumption in use, and disposal.

Manufacturing Impact

Producing electronic devices requires mining rare earth minerals and metals including lithium, cobalt, gold and tantalum. Mining operations can cause habitat destruction, water pollution and generate significant carbon emissions. The energy-intensive processes used to fabricate processors and circuit boards also contribute to carbon output. Every new device bought represents environmental cost before it has even been switched on.

Energy Consumption

Data centres power the internet, cloud storage, streaming services and online applications. Running servers continuously requires enormous amounts of electricity; cooling systems — which prevent equipment from overheating — consume additional power and water. As more services move online and global data traffic grows, the energy demands of data centres grow with it.

Individual devices also consume energy throughout their lifetimes. Keeping smartphones, laptops and televisions running adds up across billions of users. Wireless networks (mobile masts, Wi-Fi routers) require continuous power to operate.

Technology can also reduce environmental harm. Remote working and video conferencing reduce the need for commuting and business travel, cutting transport emissions. Digital documents replace paper, reducing deforestation. Smart energy-management systems in buildings use sensors and software to optimise heating and lighting, saving energy. Precision agriculture uses sensors and data analysis to apply fertilisers and water only where needed, reducing runoff. Monitoring systems can track wildlife, deforestation and pollution in real time, enabling faster responses to environmental damage.

E-Waste

E-waste (electronic waste) is one of the fastest-growing waste categories globally. Devices contain hazardous materials including lead, mercury and cadmium. When old devices end up in landfill, these substances can leach into soil and groundwater. In some parts of the world, informal recycling of e-waste exposes workers to toxic chemicals. Planned obsolescence — where manufacturers design products to have a limited lifespan or stop providing software updates after a few years — accelerates the rate at which devices are discarded.

Key Fact

E-waste is discarded electronic equipment containing hazardous materials. Planned obsolescence — designing products to become outdated quickly — increases e-waste by encouraging frequent replacement. Reducing e-waste requires longer device lifespans, easier repairability and responsible recycling schemes.

Reducing Environmental Impact

Several approaches can reduce the environmental impact of technology. Consumers can extend device lifespans by repairing rather than replacing, choosing refurbished devices, and using official recycling and take-back schemes rather than sending old electronics to general waste. Manufacturers can design products that are easier to repair, use more recycled materials, and provide software support for longer periods. Organisations can host their services on data centres that run on renewable energy or use waste heat recovery systems. Collectively, these choices reduce mining demand, energy consumption and toxic landfill.
